newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian coffee leader attacks NY "speculators".
newsitem.headline: Colombian coffee leader attacks NY "speculators".

text.p: A leader of Colombia's biggest independent coffee growers' association, Unidad Nacional Cafetera, condemned what he termed as the manipulation of international coffee prices by New York-based "speculators".

In a radio interview Sunday, the association's national coordinator Jorge Enrique Robledo, also attacked the new sliding-scale system of fixing domestic coffee prices, saying that it introduced instability into internal markets.
"The coffee business worldwide is manipulated by speculators on the New York exchange who do what they want with prices depending on their own needs," Robledo told the Caracol radio network.

The Unidad Nacional Cafetera is a loosely-woven but influential pressure group, which represents growers across nine separate provinces. It has long been critical of the National Coffee Growers' Federation, the supreme coffee authority in Colombia which controls all aspects of the industry from production through to export.

Most recently the Unidad Nacional Cafetera has pushed the government and the federation to help growers overcome high levels of indebtedness. All growers in Colombia are bound by the rules set by the federation and are linked to it through a system of regional committees.
In the face of skyrocketing international coffee prices, Colombian Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo announced a new method of calculating domestic coffee prices from the end of January.
The price paid for a 125-kg load is now revised each week and is set according to the average coffee price in the New York markets.

The domestic price rose from 221,500 pesos per 125-kg load to 383,375 pesos between Jan. 31 and March 14. But the price was cut to 363,750 pesos last Friday in the face of price corrections in the international marketplace.

"This mechanism of fixing internal prices automatically is disadvantageous for Colombian growers because its transfers the instability in markets abroad to the domestic market. If one thing is important for producers here it is for them to know what they can expect in the future," Robledo said.

Growers have also complained that the boom in international and domestic prices has not benefitted them because they have no coffee to sell until the so-called Mitaca harvest, which provides about 40 percent of the annual crop, begins at the end of this month. The main harvest takes place in October.
The Unidad Nacional Cafetera has led the call for the government to restructure cash-strapped coffee growers' debts.
Robeldo said Sunday that an effective debt relief plan should still be the main priority of the government and the National Coffee Growers' Federation.
